learning_goals: Explain what a large language model (LLM) is and its limits
Describe what RAG stands for and what each word means
List the three steps of RAG in the correct order
Tell why RAG helps and one limit of RAG

analogy.story: A student sits for an open-book exam. The student first looks up the right page in the book (retrieval). Then the student writes the answer using that page (generation).
analogy.mapping: Looking up the page is retrieval. Writing the answer is generation. The book is the knowledge base.

worked_example.setting: A college student in Delhi uses a chatbot on the college website to ask about hostel fees.
worked_example.question: What is the hostel fee for first-year B.Sc students this year?
documents: Hostel fee for 2024-25: B.Sc first year Rs 45,000 per year.
Mess charges are extra: Rs 3,000 per month.
worked_example.retrieved: Hostel fee for 2024-25: B.Sc first year Rs 45,000 per year.
worked_example.answer_without_rag: The hostel fee is around Rs 40,000 per year (old data).
worked_example.answer_with_rag: The hostel fee for first-year B.Sc students in 2024-25 is Rs 45,000 per year.

sections.heading: ## What You Will Learn
sections.goal: Show the learner the four goals of this lesson.
points: You will explain what a large language model (LLM) is and its limits (K1).
You will describe what RAG stands for and what each word means (K2).
You will list the three steps of RAG in the correct order (K3).
You will tell why RAG helps and one limit of RAG (K5, K6).

sections.heading: ## Before We Start: Some Basic Ideas
sections.goal: Explain AI, LLM, training data, knowledge cutoff, and hallucination in simple words.
points: AI is a computer program that can do tasks that need human thinking (F1).
A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a very large amount of text. It generates text by predicting the next word (F1).
Training data is the huge collection of text used to teach the LLM (F2).
Knowledge cutoff is the date when the training data stops. The LLM does not know events after that date (F2).
Hallucination is when the LLM makes up answers that sound confident but are wrong (F4).
An LLM does not know private information like your college fee list (F3).

sections.heading: ## What Is RAG?
sections.goal: Define RAG and explain the meaning of each word in the name.
points: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (F5).
Retrieval means finding and fetching relevant pieces of information (F5).
Augmented means added to or made stronger. The retrieved text is added to the question (F5).
Generation means the LLM writes the answer using the question plus the retrieved text (F5).
RAG does not change the model. The model weights stay the same (F9).

sections.heading: ## Why Does RAG Matter?
sections.goal: List the benefits of RAG and contrast with fine-tuning.
points: RAG lets the LLM use up-to-date and private information (F11).
RAG reduces made-up answers but does not remove them fully (F11).
Answers can show their sources (F11).
RAG is cheaper and faster than retraining the model (F11).
Knowledge is easy to update by changing the documents (F11).
Fine-tuning trains the model further and changes its weights. It is slower and costlier (F10).
RAG is usually the better first choice for new or changing facts (F10).

sections.heading: ## How Does RAG Work?
sections.goal: Explain the preparation step and the three question-time steps in order.
points: Preparation (indexing) is done before questions arrive (F7).
Collect documents, split them into small pieces called chunks (F7).
A chunk is a small piece of text (F7).
Turn each chunk into an embedding using an embedding model (F7).
An embedding is a list of numbers that captures the meaning of the text (F7).
An embedding model is a tool that changes text into embeddings (F7).
Store embeddings in a vector database (F7).
A vector database is a searchable index that holds vectors (F7).
A vector is a list of numbers that represents meaning (F7).
Question-time step 1: Retrieve. The user question is turned into an embedding. The system finds chunks with similar meaning using semantic search (F8).
Semantic search means searching by meaning, not just keywords (F8).
Question-time step 2: Augment. The retrieved chunks are placed into the prompt with the question and an instruction (F8).
A prompt is the text you give to the LLM to get an answer (F8).
Context is the extra information added to the prompt (F8).
Question-time step 3: Generate. The LLM writes the answer from the question plus the retrieved context (F8).
The LLM can also cite the sources it used (F8).

sections.heading: ## Example: College Hostel Fee Chatbot
sections.goal: Show a concrete Indian example of RAG in action.
points: Setting: A college student in Delhi uses a chatbot on the college website (worked_example.setting).
Question: What is the hostel fee for first-year B.Sc students this year? (worked_example.question).
Documents in the knowledge base: three short snippets (worked_example.documents).
Retrieved snippet: the one with the current year fee (worked_example.retrieved).
Answer without RAG: the LLM uses old training data and says Rs 40,000 (worked_example.answer_without_rag).
Answer with RAG: the LLM uses the retrieved snippet and says Rs 45,000 (worked_example.answer_with_rag).

sections.heading: ## Key Words to Remember
sections.goal: List the important terms with one-line definitions.
points: Large language model (LLM): an AI model trained on huge text that predicts the next word.
Training data: the text used to teach the LLM.
Knowledge cutoff: the date when training data stops.
Hallucination: when the LLM makes up wrong but confident answers.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): a method that finds relevant text and adds it to the prompt before the LLM answers.
Retrieval: finding relevant pieces of information.
Augment: adding the retrieved text to the prompt.
Generate: the LLM writing the answer.
Chunk: a small piece of a document.
Embedding: a list of numbers that captures the meaning of text.
Embedding model: a tool that turns text into embeddings.
Vector: a list of numbers that represents meaning.
Vector database: a searchable index that stores vectors.
Semantic search: searching by meaning, not just keywords.
Prompt: the text you give to the LLM to get an answer.
Context: extra information added to the prompt.
Fine-tuning: training the model further on new examples to change its weights.
Weights: the learned internal numbers of the model.
Retraining: teaching the model again from scratch or continuing training to change its weights.

sections.heading: ## Quick Check
sections.goal: Five simple questions to test understanding.
points: What does LLM stand for? Answer: large language model.
What are the three steps of RAG in order? Answer: retrieve, augment, generate.
Does RAG change the model weights? Answer: No, RAG does not change the model weights.
What is one benefit of RAG? Answer: It lets the LLM use up-to-date and private information.
What is one limit of RAG? Answer: The answer depends on the quality of what is retrieved.

sections.heading: ## Summary
sections.goal: Recap the main points in a few sentences.
points: An LLM is trained on a fixed set of text and has a knowledge cutoff. It does not know private data and can hallucinate.
RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It adds a retrieval step before the LLM generates an answer.
The three steps are retrieve, augment, generate. Preparation creates chunks, embeddings, and a vector database.
RAG gives fresh and private information, shows sources, and avoids retraining. But the answer is only as good as the retrieved chunks.

quiz.q: In RAG, what happens in the retrieval step?
quiz.a: The system finds the most relevant chunks from the knowledge base for the user question.
No, RAG does not change the model weights. It only adds retrieved text to the prompt.
A small piece of a document created during the preparation step.

quiz.q: Why might a RAG answer still be wrong?
quiz.a: If the retrieval step returns the wrong or outdated chunks, the answer can be wrong.
